meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The sad truth is that most evil is done by people who never make up their minds to be good or evil'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Hannah Arendt, from The Life of the Mind (1977–78) — though the circulating wording is a slight paraphrase of her original line.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This is a genuine Arendt line, from her final work The Life of the Mind, Vol. 1: Thinking (1977–78). Her original sentence reads “The sad truth of the matter is that most evil is done by people who never made up their minds to be or do either evil or good” — the version circulating online lightly compresses it, but the thought and nearly the exact words are hers.

source.excerpt: The sad truth of the matter is that most evil is done by people who never made up their minds to be or do either evil or good.
trail: Wikiquote lists the line among its sourced Arendt quotations, citing The Life of the Mind (1978), “Thinking” — wording it as “…never made up their minds to be or do either evil or good.”
The quotation reference WIST pins it to Vol. 1 “Thinking,” Part 3, ch. 18 “The Two-in-One,” and notes it first appeared in a 1977 New Yorker essay (“Thinking — III,” 5 Dec 1977).
QuotePark carries the same original wording, attributed to The Life of the Mind (1978), “Thinking.”
Goodreads circulates the compressed popular wording, also crediting The Life of the Mind.
source.excerptNote: Arendt’s original, per her posthumously published The Life of the Mind. The popular internet version — “most evil is done by people who never make up their minds to be good or evil” — is a shortened paraphrase of this sentence.
source.rightsHolder: The Estate of Hannah Arendt and her publisher Harcourt Brace Jovanovich (now HarperCollins)
source.rightsNote: The Life of the Mind was first published in 1977–1978, editing by Mary McCarthy after Arendt’s 1975 death. As a work first published well after 1930, it remains under U.S. copyright; the line is not in the public domain.

author.name: Hannah Arendt
author.heading: Hannah Arendt
author.bio: Hannah Arendt was a German-born American political theorist whose work on totalitarianism, power, and moral judgment shaped 20th-century political thought. Reporting on Adolf Eichmann’s 1961 trial, she coined the phrase the banality of evil to describe how ordinary, unthinking people enable atrocity. This quote comes from The Life of the Mind, the ambitious study of thinking, willing and judging she left unfinished at her death in 1975.

misattribution.heading: Right author, drifted wording
misattribution.intro: Unusually for a “famous name” quote, the attribution here is correct — Arendt really wrote it. What drifted is the wording.

items.why: The most-shared line — “most evil is done by people who never make up their minds to be good or evil” — compresses Arendt’s fuller sentence. Her original (per WIST and Wikiquote) reads “…never made up their minds to be or do either evil or good,” and opens “The sad truth of the matter is…”

misattribution.truthLine: The idea — and nearly the exact words — are genuinely Arendt’s, from The Life of the Mind; only the phrasing was tidied in circulation.

context.heading: Thinking as a defense against evil
lead: Arendt wrote this in The Life of the Mind, the book she was still finishing when she died. It grew directly out of her reporting on the 1961 Eichmann trial and her controversial idea of the “banality of evil” — the observation that great wrongs are often committed not by monsters but by unreflective people who simply never stop to think.

In this passage she argues that most evil comes not from those who deliberately choose it but from people who never make the choice at all — who fail to engage in the inner dialogue she calls thinking. It is a claim about absence rather than malice: the failure to think, she suggests, is itself a moral condition.
